title: GRE Verbal: The Three Question Types
summary: Text Completion, Sentence Equivalence and Reading Comprehension — what each tests and the fastest way to attack it.

nodes.label: Sentence Equivalence
nodes.note: Pick TWO words → same meaning sentence

chunks.heading: Text Completion — read the clue, then the blank
chunks.body: A short passage has **one to three blanks**; choose the word that best fits each (no partial credit for multi-blank — all must be right). The trick: find the **clue and the signpost** (a word like 'although', 'because', 'yet') that tells you whether the blank agrees or contrasts with the rest.
chunks.realExample: 'Although praised as ___, the plan was actually reckless.' 'Although' signals contrast, so the blank must be positive — 'prudent'. Predict your own word before reading the options.
chunks.memoryHook: Find the signpost (although/because) first. It tells you the blank's direction.

chunks.heading: Sentence Equivalence — two words, one meaning
chunks.body: One blank, **six options — pick the TWO** that both fit AND produce **sentences with the same meaning**. So you're hunting a **synonym pair**, not just any two workable words.
chunks.realExample: If 'gregarious' fits, look for its partner 'sociable' — two options that mean the same. Two words that both fit but mean different things is the classic trap answer.
chunks.memoryHook: Two answers that are SYNONYMS. Find the pair, not just two that fit.

chunks.heading: Reading Comprehension — answer from the text, not your view
chunks.body: Passages come with detail, inference and 'purpose' questions. Every answer must be **provable from the passage** — the right choice is supported by specific lines; wrong ones are true-in-the-world but unsupported, or distort the text.
chunks.realExample: Question: 'The author implies…' → find the exact sentence that backs the choice. If you can't point to it, it's probably the trap that 'sounds reasonable' but isn't stated.
chunks.memoryHook: If you can't underline the proof in the passage, it's not the answer.

chunks.heading: Vocabulary in context wins Verbal
chunks.body: GRE Verbal rewards **knowing words in context** far more than obscure trivia. Build vocabulary through **word families and roots**, and always learn a word inside a sentence — that's exactly how the test uses it.
chunks.realExample: Learning 'laconic' as 'using few words' inside 'his laconic reply' sticks better than a bare definition — and that's the form Text Completion tests.
chunks.memoryHook: Learn words in sentences, not on flashcards alone. Context is the test.

recall.q: How many blanks can a Text Completion question have, and is there partial credit?
recall.a: One to three blanks, and there's no partial credit — every blank must be correct.

recall.q: What must the two answers in Sentence Equivalence have in common?
recall.a: They must be a synonym pair that both fit and produce sentences with the same meaning.

recall.q: How do you identify the direction of a Text Completion blank?
recall.a: Find the signpost word (e.g. although, because, yet) that tells you whether the blank agrees or contrasts with the clue.

recall.q: What makes an answer correct in Reading Comprehension?
recall.a: It must be provable from specific lines in the passage — not merely true in general.

recall.q: What's the most effective way to build GRE vocabulary?
recall.a: Learn words in context via sentences, word families and roots — the way the test uses them.
